Chapter 2: Giving Others an “A” and Transforming Relationships
Think about the world we live in—schools, offices, even families. Almost everywhere, people are measured, graded, and ranked. There’s this constant pressure to perform, to earn approval, and to avoid making mistakes. Sound familiar? It’s no wonder so many of us hold back, second-guess ourselves, or keep quiet about our best ideas.
But what if that whole system of judgment... could just be put aside, even for a little while? What if, instead of waiting for people to prove themselves, we just gave everyone the benefit of the doubt from the very start?
Imagine walking into a college class on the first day, and the instructor announces that every single student will get the highest grade possible—no matter what. The only thing you need to do is write a letter, dated months in the future, describing who you became to truly earn that grade. At first, you can almost hear the disbelief. Some students wonder if it’s a trick. Others feel a wave of relief wash over them.
As the weeks go on, something pretty remarkable happens. Without that fear of failure hanging over their heads, students start taking chances. They ask more questions. They support each other. Suddenly, it’s not about competition anymore—it’s about growth and curiosity. That’s the heart of giving an “A” in advance. It’s not about lowering standards or pretending everything’s perfect. It’s about seeing people, not just as they are, but as they could be. It’s a way of saying, “Hey, I believe in your potential, and I want to treat you from that place.” And you know what? Most people, when they feel trusted like that, really rise to the occasion. They feel valued, seen, and ready to bring their best selves forward.
Let’s look at a real-world example in the workplace. Picture a team leader who’s had a tough time with a colleague. Instead of focusing on old mistakes or frustrations, the leader decides to assume positive intent. All of a sudden, meetings feel less tense. The colleague, sensing the change, starts to contribute more openly. What once felt like a strained relationship begins to thaw. Turns out, a lot of that old conflict came from mutual suspicion and defensiveness—habits that can change when someone’s willing to see the best in the other.
The same thing happens at home. Parents sometimes get stuck measuring their kids against grades, trophies, or milestones. All that constant evaluation? It can really wear down trust and stifle growth. But when a parent chooses to see their child as already worthy and already capable, something shifts. The child feels safe to explore, to make mistakes, and to grow at their own pace.
Now, I’ll be honest: relating to people this way isn’t always easy. Those old habits of judgment run deep, and the fear of being taken advantage of can be strong. But here’s what’s amazing—when you give someone an “A,” you invite them to step into a bigger, brighter version of themselves. Relationships stop being about keeping score and start being about mutual support and discovery.
This isn’t about ignoring problems or pretending everyone’s perfect. It’s about choosing to relate to others from a place of possibility, seeing beyond what’s right in front of you, and nurturing what’s best in each person. Over time, this simple shift can transform not only your relationships, but entire communities and organizations.
So, here’s the key takeaway: people tend to live up—or down—to the expectations we set for them. By choosing to expect the best, you’re helping to create an environment where growth, trust, and real connection can flourish.
